Scale Patterns

Scale exercises written out for any key, scale, meter, style and instrument: scales, broken intervals, groups, Hanon, arpeggios, jazz digital patterns and enclosures, with fingerings, slide positions, valves or strings under the notes.

Exercise

ABC






Practice notes


    

    

    

    On your instrument
    

      

      The instrument notes are general teaching advice, not yet checked against a source; more on each band instrument is coming.
      

      

      

      How it works
      

        

      • Key and spelling. Every note takes its letter from the scale’s own degrees, so G♯ harmonic minor has its F𝄪 and the blues scale has both the ♭5 and the 5. The key signature is the scale’s mode on the tonic (Dorian on D: no sharps or flats); harmonic and melodic minor use the natural minor’s, as printed scale books do. Enharmonic keys (F♯ / G♭) are spelled with the fewer accidentals, and for a transposing instrument with the fewer in the key you read.
        • 

      • Transposing instruments read written pitch (B♭ instruments a step up, E♭ alto a sixth up, horn in F a fifth up, guitar and bass an octave up); playback sounds at concert pitch.
        • 

      • Patterns move up the scale one step at a time, then down. “Mirror” turns the figure upside down on the way down (Hanon’s way); off, the same shape moves down (the jazz way, so an enclosure still lands on its target from both sides).
        • 

      • Swing is written as straight eighths; the playback swings them, and with the band the band’s own swing feel plays.
        • 

      • Hanon. Nos. 1–20 (The Virtuoso Pianist, Part I) are played note for note, with Hanon’s fingering, from the Mutopia Project’s edition (after Schirmer, 1900), read by a script. They keep Hanon’s two octaves; on another scale the same degrees are used, and on a scale that isn’t seven notes the figure changes shape.
        • 

      

      

      

      Works Cited
      


      

      Aebersold, Jamey. Scale Syllabus. Jamey Aebersold Jazz, www.jazzbooks.com/mm5/download/FREE-scale-syllabus.pdf.
      

      Hanon, Charles-Louis. “Exercise No. 2.” The Virtuoso Pianist, Part I, Hanon-Online, hanon-online.com/the-virtuoso-pianist-part-i/hanon-exercise-n-2/hanon-exercise-n-2-in-g. Hanon’s practice directions (lift the fingers, play each note distinctly, begin at 60).
      

      Hanon, Charles-Louis. The Virtuoso Pianist (Part I). 1873. Edited by Steve Taylor and Javier Ruiz-Alma after the Schirmer edition of 1900, Mutopia Project, 2015, www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2037. CC BY-SA 4.0. Exercises 1–20 read note for note into apps/shared/hanon-part1.js.
